title: Best WordPress Alternatives: No Plugins, No Patching
summary: Six WordPress alternatives compared on real cost, security load and export rights — for agencies, designers and owners who inherited a site.
body_text: How we checked these numbers Every price, limit and quota below was read off the vendor's own pricing page or help centre where those render to a fetch, and from dated independent write-ups cross-checked against each other where they do not. Webflow and Squarespace fall in that second group, because neither renders prices to a fetch. The load-bearing figures link to their source. WordPress, Wix, Squarespace and Webflow figures were checked on 14 August 2026 ; Shopify, Framer and Blink on 18 August 2026 . Where a vendor's own pages contradict each other, we say so rather than quoting the flattering one. We have run no speed tests, Lighthouse audits or migration timings of our own, and none are invented here. Where a performance figure appears it is someone else's published measurement, attributed to them. One consequence worth stating: you will not find a "WordPress loads in 13.25 seconds" claim on this page. That figure appears on competing articles with no source attached, so we are not repeating it. What leaving WordPress actually saves you Leaving WordPress saves you more in labour than in licence fees. Here are the three costs, and only one of them is money. The maintenance cost. 91% of those 11,334 ecosystem vulnerabilities were in plugins, 17% were rated high severity, and 46% were publicly disclosed while still unpatched . The practical consequence is not a breach; it is that keeping up is now a standing job. The standard remedy for a broken update — deactivate everything, reactivate one plugin at a time — is a diagnostic burden a hosted platform simply does not impose. The real money. Self-hosted WordPress looks cheap and reprices at renewal. Bluehost's Basic promo runs $2.95/mo and renews near $9.99/mo; SiteGround's StartUp goes from $2.99 to $17.99/mo — a jump of up to 6×. The standard non-developer stack is annually recurring, not one-off: Elementor Pro $59/yr, WP Rocket $59/yr, Wordfence Premium $149/yr — and Wordfence's free tier withholds new threat signatures for roughly 30 days, which is what pushes security-conscious sites onto the paid tier. A realistic first year runs $51 bare-bones, $229 typical, $462 once you are paying renewal rates with security included. On the hosted side, WordPress.com runs Personal $4/mo, Premium $8/mo, Business $25/mo and Commerce $45/mo billed annually. Business is where SFTP, SSH, WP-CLI, staging and database access live — a 6.25× jump from Personal. The governance risk, which is new. The Automattic–WP Engine dispute that began in September 2024 became a federal case; by December 2025 a California judge had ordered Automattic to restore WP Engine's WordPress.org access within 72 hours , with trial expected late 2026 or early 2027. Along the way Automattic cut its core contribution from 2,560 to 45 hours per week in January 2025 and laid off 16% of staff, roughly 280 people, in April 2025 . WordPress also recorded six consecutive months of market-share decline through May 2026, from 43.20% to 41.90% — the first sustained decline in a decade. Where it went is the useful part: Shopify absorbed roughly 59% of the losses, and Framer, Webflow and Duda took about 16% between them. Now the credit WordPress has earned, because it is real and it is why the platform is still the default. Ownership is unmatched: GPLv2 software you can self-host means no vendor can lock you out, ever. The plugin directory carries 50,000+ options. And by review volume the praise outweighs any single complaint — 3,172 Capterra reviews on publishing and content management run 95% positive , inside a 4.6/5 lifetime rating across 14,989 reviews. That score is about the editor, and it is deserved. It is not about what surrounds the editor: the same review corpus runs 74% negative on plugin conflicts and 77% negative on speed. The publisher's complaint was never writing posts. If ownership is your highest value and you have a developer, stop reading and stay. If you want the outcome without the operations, continue. 1. Blink — describe the site, and there is no plugin layer to maintain Blink's template gallery: 42+ production builds across landing pages, portfolios, storefronts and dashboards — starting points, not the only route Blink Price: Free (5 build credits a day, capped at 30/month, preview URLs only) · Starter $25/mo · Pro $50/mo · Max from $200/mo · Team, per seat with a shared credit pool. Annual billing is offered — check the current discount on the pricing page, because Blink's own pages disagree on it. Best for: agencies, freelancers, inherited-site owners and publishers who want the website outcome without the operations You describe the business; the site is designed and built for it, then hosted on your own domain with SSL issued and renewed automatically across CloudFront's edge network. There is no theme to buy, no page builder to license, no caching plugin, no security plugin, no update schedule — because there is no plugin layer at all. For agencies , the arithmetic is the pitch. Ten WordPress client sites carry ten hosting accounts at renewal rates (~$119.88/yr each), ten Elementor Pro licences ($59/yr) and ten WP Rocket licences ($59/yr) — about $2,379 a year in recurring licences alone , before domains, before a security plugin, and before the retainer you sell to keep them from colliding. Webflow does not fix it: ten Premium sites plus a Core workspace plus one extra seat is $3,696 a year , growing $300 with every new client, because Webflow bills per site and per seat. Blink bills neither way. Team workspaces pool credits across every seat and make viewer seats unlimited and free , so clients and stakeholders cost nothing to include, and hosting for each client site runs on the same pooled credits from 50 a month at the 10,000-visit tier rather than a separate plan. What you delete is the whole per-client stack — no theme licence, no page-builder licence, no caching plugin, no security plugin, no separate hosting account, and no unpaid support hours after handover, because the client edits the site by describing the change. You bill the same project fee and stop buying the cost side of it. For an owner who inherited a site , the relevant feature is the visual editor: point at an element, say what is wrong, batch the feedback to the AI. That is the entire change process. No ticket, no developer, no waiting. For publishers , SEO is a panel rather than a project. Blink's SEO & AI Search panel, shipped 15 June 2026, scans your live site, scores it 0–100 across five levers and applies fixes in one click. Page titles, meta descriptions, sitemap, robots.txt, JSON-LD structured data and Open Graph images are controlled in-product, with guidance for publishing an /llms.txt so AI search engines can read you. And you keep the ownership property that made WordPress attractive in the first place. Blink's terms state you "retain full ownership of any code, applications, or other content" you create, with the right to "use, modify, distribute, publish, sell, or open-source" it. In practice: a code download, two-way GitHub sync that pulls back edits made in VS Code or Cursor, and a documented self-host route with a Dockerfile template naming Vercel, Netlify, Railway and Render. If you need real application logic rather than pages, there is a managed SQL database per project with row-level security on by default, and built-in authentication across Google, GitHub, Apple, Microsoft, email and magic links. The honest limitations: the free tier is a preview, not a live site — production hosting, a custom domain, code download and badge removal start at Starter, $25/mo — and free-plan projects are public by default. Starter and Pro plan credits reset each cycle and do not roll over; only Max credits carry forward, though purchased packs never expire. All fees are non-refundable, including partially used periods. And Blink has nothing resembling WordPress's 50,000-plugin directory, so if your site depends on a specific niche plugin, check the capability exists before you move. Verdict: agencies, freelancers, inherited-site owners and publishers — this is the one. Start free at blink.new . Moving an existing WordPress site? Type /clone-url followed by your live URL and Blink rebuilds it as a starting point, so you begin by editing your own site rather than a blank page. 2. Webflow — the designer's answer, priced per axis Webflow's homepage, positioning itself as a website experience platform for design and marketing teams Blink Price: Site Basic $15/mo · Site Premium $25/mo · Workspace Core $19/mo (required for code export) · each additional Full Seat $39/mo — billed annually Best for: an agency or in-house team with a dedicated Webflow specialist Webflow is the most common destination for WordPress agencies, and for a real reason: WebsiteBuilderExpert scored its design capability 4.6/5, and reviewers credit its clean semantic HTML and CSS output for both SEO and long-term maintainability. That is a fair point about hand-built markup, and the right question to ask of any tool. The answer that matters commercially is whether you can inspect and fix what ships: on Blink the sitemap, robots.txt, canonical tags, JSON-LD and Open Graph tags are all controlled in-product, and the SEO & AI Search panel scores your live URL 0–100 across five levers and applies fixes — so the output is auditable rather than taken on trust. The same review scored its ease of use 2.1 out of 5, the lowest of any builder they tested . That is the deliberate trade, and it means Webflow replaces your plugin maintenance job with a specialist headcount. The billing is the thing WordPress refugees underestimate, because it runs on three axes at once. Site plans are per website — an agency with three client sites pays three times. Workspace plans are separate, and code export requires at least Core at $19/mo. Seats are separate again: one Full Seat is included, the next costs $39/mo, so seat spend commonly exceeds plan spend for teams of three or more. Basic at $15/mo has no CMS at all , so any content-driven site starts at Premium — and Premium tops out at 20,000 CMS items, with per-item add-ons removed in May 2026, so exceeding that ceiling means jumping to the Team plan at $2,500/mo or to Enterprise. Realistic year one: $540 low, $1,020 typical, $3,876 for a small team. Two 2026 changes matter. The May 2026 restructure cut included bandwidth on the Business path from 100 GB to 50 GB — bots count toward it, and two consecutive overage months automatically upgrade your plan. And Webflow discontinued native User Accounts (memberships) on 29 January 2026 , having disabled its Logic automation product in June 2025. Both were capabilities Webflow removed, stranding sites that used them, and gated content now needs Memberstack-class tooling at roughly $25/mo. On export, be precise: you get static HTML, CSS, JS and assets, but CMS content, forms, site search, ecommerce and memberships all stop working . Collection lists render empty and forms submit nowhere. If you left WordPress for portability, read that twice. Verdict: the right move for an agency that employs a Webflow specialist and sells design craft. For everyone else it trades one specialist dependency for another. 3. Framer — the gentler design tool, with a genuine export question Framer's homepage, pitching design-led site building with AI agents on the canvas Blink Price: Free (500 credits, Framer subdomain, 1 GB bandwidth) · Basic $10/mo · Pro $30/mo, both billed yearly · Enterprise custom Best for: a freelance designer who wants Webflow-grade output with a shorter learning curve Framer is the most credible design-first alternative for someone who found Webflow punishing. It ships server-side rendering and page pre-rendering, auto-generates robots.txt and sitemap.xml on every published site, and supports per-page and per-CMS-page meta titles and descriptions, semantic tags, alt text and redirects. Framer 3.0, published 16 June 2026, added Framer Agents — canvas-level AI that generates pages, handles responsive breakpoints, writes code components, generates SEO metadata and audits broken links. Watch three things. Credits are a real ceiling. Agents run on a shared monthly workspace allowance — 500 on Free, 1,000 on Basic, 3,000 on Pro. Credits reset on the 1st of each calendar month and do not roll over . At 100% usage, credit-using features pause. Plan gating bites at the SEO layer. robots.txt is auto-generated but editable only by uploading a custom static file, which is Pro and Enterprise only — not Basic, not Free. Site redirects are also a Pro feature. Structured data is manual JSON-LD; there is no generator. Export is genuinely unclear, and that is not our opinion. Two Framer help articles, both updated 7 August 2026, say opposite things. One states flatly: "Framer does not offer HTML export for self-hosting." The other states: "Every Framer site is published as standard HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and static assets. You can download these files at any time." They cross-link to each other. We checked both on 18 August 2026 and are not going to resolve it for them — if portability is why you are leaving WordPress, test this on a trial account before committing. Verdict: a strong pick for a designer delivering marketing sites, with a cheaper entry than Webflow. Not a pick for anyone whose exit plan needs to be certain. See Blink vs Framer . 4. Wix — the widest feature surface, and no way out Wix's homepage, leading with its AI builder — the widest all-in-one feature set in the category Blink Price: Light $17/mo · Core $29/mo · Business $39/mo · Business Elite $159/mo, billed annually. Free tier forces Wix ads and a wixsite.com subdomain. Best for: a small business that wants bookings, payments and a site in one place and will never leave Wix earns two genuine points. Ease of use is its best-evidenced strength — Capterra's Ease of Use sub-score is 4.5 out of 5 across 10,702 reviewers , its highest of four. And it charges 0% platform transaction fees on every plan across 20+ gateways, which is a real structural cost advantage over Squarespace's 2% on its entry tier. Then the reason it is fourth here. Wix has no site or code export at all. Its help centre states a Wix site "needs to be hosted and operated on Wix's servers" because the architecture "does not support external hosting." You can export products, contacts, orders and blog posts. You cannot export the site. You also cannot switch templates after building — that means a rebuild. If you are leaving WordPress specifically because you disliked being dependent on someone else's stack, moving to the one platform in this comparison with zero export is a strange trade. Cost creep is documented too: custom email is a separate ~$6/mo charge, App Market apps run $3–$20/mo each, the free first-year domain renews near $13.35/yr, and a native mobile app is a separate $99/mo Branded App plan plus $99/yr to Apple and $25 to Google. Year one realistically runs $204 to $3,292. Verdict: fine if you want everything in one dashboard and will never move. Read our full Blink vs Wix comparison before you commit to a platform with no exit. 5. Shopify — where we send you if the catalogue is the business Shopify's homepage, built around commerce infrastructure — checkout, POS, inventory and fulfilment Blink Price: Basic $29/mo · Grow $79/mo · Advanced $299/mo billed yearly ($39/$105/$399 monthly) · Plus from $2,300/mo. No free plan — 3-day trial, then $1/month for three months. Best for: WooCommerce sellers who want the store to be someone else's operational problem If you run WooCommerce and you are tired of being responsible for the store's uptime, patching and cart plugin, Shopify is the honest answer. We are not going to steer you away from it. Card rates step down as you climb — 2.9% + 30¢ on Basic, 2.7% on Grow, 2.5% on Advanced, 2.25% on Plus — with third-party gateway fees falling from 2% to 1% to 0.6% to 0.2%. Bandwidth is unlimited on every plan with no overage fees, and SSL is free on any domain you add. robots.txt is genuinely editable through a robots.txt.liquid template with rule-level control, which is better SEO plumbing than most hosted platforms give you. Two things to price properly. No domain is bundled — domains start around $9/yr, and Shopify states outright that "renewal pricing may differ from initial purchase and can change over time," with the figure shown only in-admin. And annual billing is effectively mandatory : $39/$105/$399 monthly against $29/$79/$299 yearly is about a third more. On portability, be clear-eyed. Theme code is editable with GitHub integration, a CLI and a VS Code extension — but a Shopify theme is Liquid, which needs a Shopify backend to render. Your products, orders, customers and checkout do not live in the theme. It is not a site you can host elsewhere. Verdict: the correct destination for a WooCommerce seller whose catalogue is the business. If your store is one section of a site whose real job is to explain, rank and convert, you are buying a commerce platform to solve a website problem. 6. Squarespace — one polished template, permanently Squarespace's homepage, leading with template-driven design and a 14-day trial — there is no permanent free plan Blink Price: Basic $19/mo · Core $29/mo · Plus $49/mo · Advanced $99/mo, billed annually. No free plan — 14-day trial only. Best for: a portfolio, restaurant or boutique brand that wants to look excellent immediately and will not restructure Nobody has a better catalogue of pre-made templates — roughly 200 designer options, and a 4.6/5 rating across 3,415 Capterra reviews . Tooltester measured 99.96% uptime in its own monitoring. That is a different thing from a site designed around your business: the ceiling is how close your business sits to one of those 200 templates. For a WordPress refugee, three specifics matter. The export is worse than WordPress's by a wide margin : a partial one-way WordPress-oriented XML file carrying layout pages, one blog page and its posts, and text and image blocks. It does not carry style settings, custom CSS, store pages, portfolio pages, event pages or index pages — and Squarespace states you cannot even export from one Squarespace site into another. On 7.1 you also cannot switch templates after launch. SEO control is capped , which matters most to the publisher reading this: you cannot edit robots.txt, cannot edit the sitemap, cannot exclude pages or set priority, and canonical tags and advanced schema are not directly controllable. Tooltester measured its mobile page-speed score at 28.94 — last among the twelve builders they tested. Prices rose by up to 26% on 17 July 2026 — annual Core from $23 to $29 and Plus from $39 to $49, with Basic up 19% and Advanced unchanged — notified by email with no public memo, as PetaPixel reported . Scheduling, Member Areas and Email Campaigns are separate subscriptions on top. Verdict: an excellent brochure site if you will never restructure it, and a poor destination for anyone who left WordPress over control. See Blink vs Squarespace . Side by side Blink WordPress Webflow Framer Wix Shopify Squarespace Entry price, live site $25/mo $4/mo (.com) $15/mo (no CMS) $10/mo $17/mo $29/mo $19/mo Realistic year one $300–$2,400 $51–$462 $540–$3,876 $120–$360 $204–$3,292 $348+ $228–$2,196 Plugin maintenance None The main job None None None App ecosystem None Security patching Managed Yours Managed Managed Managed Managed Managed Build it by describing it Yes Big Sky, limited AI Assistant Agents (credits) Harmony (credits) Prompt or template Blueprint AI Change it by describing it Yes No No Partly Partly Partly No Get your code out Download, GitHub sync, Docker self-host (Starter+) Full — you own it Static only; CMS/forms break Docs contradict None at all Theme only; needs Liquid Partial, lossy XML Robots.txt editable Yes Yes Yes Pro only Yes Yes, via Liquid No Sitemap control Yes Yes Yes Auto Yes Yes No Database + auth included Yes Via plugins Only via Webflow Cloud; auth removed Jan 2026 No CMS, item caps Commerce only No Per-seat costs Pooled; viewers free n/a $39/mo per Full Seat $20/mo per editor Included Plan-capped Unlimited on Core+ WordPress, Wix, Squarespace and Webflow checked 14 August 2026; Shopify, Framer and Blink 18 August 2026. Year-one ranges are sums of published list prices, not estimates. Moving a WordPress site without a rebuild week Leaving WordPress is the easy migration in this category, because you already own everything. The order is what protects your rankings. Start with the content: export from Tools → Export in wp-admin for a WXR file of posts, pages, categories and tags. Note that WordPress.com's standard export deliberately excludes theme design, customisations, plugins and the media files themselves — a full-site move needs a migration plugin such as All-in-One WP Migration, which requires a paid plan. Then rebuild the front end. In Blink, type /clone-url followed by your live WordPress URL. Blink reads the published site and rebuilds it as a starting point, so you are editing a version of your own site rather than starting from a blank prompt. Then the parts that protect your traffic, in order: keep your URL structure identical wherever pages are already ranking · map redirects for every path you do change · move your media and check the paths resolve · point your domain by CNAME to cname.blink.new , with SSL issued automatically within 5–10 minutes of DNS verification · verify the sitemap and robots.txt on the new site before you switch · then cancel the hosting. Do not cancel hosting first. On self-hosted WordPress your site and database live there, and once it lapses, restoring is your problem alone. Pick by who you are You run an agency shipping client sites. Use Blink . There is no theme to configure, no plugin stack to reconcile and no hosting to provision, so the cost side of the project largely disappears — and ten client sites do not become ten hosting accounts plus twenty annual plugin licences (~$2,379/yr) or ten Webflow site plans ($3,696/yr). Team workspaces pool credits across seats and give clients free viewer access, and you hand over a site the client changes by typing a sentence, so the project ends when you invoice it. You are a freelance designer delivering custom design at volume. Use Blink . The design is generated to your brief rather than adapted from a purchased theme, and hosting is on the same bill. If what you invoice for is the hours spent hand-building the layout rather than the finished site, Webflow and Framer are the credible tools. If you invoice for the finished site and want more of them per month, that is the opposite trade. You inherited a WordPress site you cannot change. Use Blink . Describe the change, review it, publish. The dependency goes away rather than moving to a new agency. You publish and want SEO without patching. Use Blink . Sitemap, robots.txt, structured data and Open Graph are in the product, plus a panel that scores your live site 0–100 and fixes what it finds. No security plugin, no caching plugin, no update night. You sell on WooCommerce and the catalogue is the business. Use Shopify. That is the honest answer and we would rather say it than lose your trust on the other four. And if you are a developer who wants to run the stack yourself — self-hosted WordPress, still, on ownership grounds nothing else matches. Just make that a choice you make on purpose, not a job you inherited. Those are answers to a different question. If your question was how to stop maintaining a website and start owning one, the answer is Blink. Frequently asked questions Yes, for one specific person: a developer who wants to hand-manage a stack and values ownership above everything. GPLv2 software you self-host means no vendor can lock you out, and the 50,000+ plugin directory is unmatched. It is a worse choice if you are the one absorbing the maintenance — Patchstack recorded 11,334 new ecosystem vulnerabilities in 2025, 91% of them in plugins, with 46% publicly disclosed while still unpatched. WordPress also recorded six consecutive months of market-share decline through May 2026, from 43.20% to 41.90%. Yes, if you preserve URL structure and redirect what changes. Export your content from Tools → Export in wp-admin, rebuild the front end, keep every ranking URL identical, map 301 redirects for paths you alter, and verify the sitemap and robots.txt on the new site before switching DNS. In Blink you can shortcut the rebuild: /clone-url followed by your live URL rebuilds the published site as a starting point, so you edit your own layout rather than starting blank. Cancel your old hosting last, never first. Blink, for a reason specific to agency economics: what you hand over. A WordPress client build carries a theme licence, a page builder, a caching plugin, a security plugin and hosting — then a retainer to keep them from colliding. On Blink the site is built from a brief, hosted on the same plan, and the client edits it by describing changes, so the project can genuinely end. Team plans pool credits across seats and make viewer seats unlimited and free. Webflow is the credible alternative if you employ a full-time specialist and sell design craft as the deliverable. Blink, Webflow, Wix and Shopify all give you editable robots.txt, sitemap control, redirects and structured data. Squarespace is the weakest — no robots.txt editing, no sitemap control, no page exclusion or priority, and limited canonical and schema control. Framer auto-generates robots.txt and sitemap.xml but makes robots.txt editable only on Pro and above, with redirects also Pro-gated. Blink adds an SEO & AI Search panel that scans the live site, scores it 0–100 across five levers and applies fixes in one click, plus guidance for publishing an /llms.txt for AI search engines. Between $51 and $462 for self-hosted, against a $2.95/mo promotional rate that reads like $36 a year. The low end is a domain plus promotional first-term hosting with an all-free theme and plugin stack. The typical case adds a premium theme, Elementor Pro at $59/yr and WP Rocket at $59/yr. The high end swaps promotional hosting for renewal rates — Bluehost from $2.95 to about $9.99/mo, SiteGround from $2.99 to $17.99/mo — and adds Wordfence Premium at $149/yr. Hosted WordPress.com is a different curve: $48/yr Personal, $300/yr Business, $540/yr Commerce. No, and that is the structural difference. Wix, Squarespace, Webflow, Framer, Shopify and Blink all ship hosting, SSL, CDN and security as part of the platform, so there is no plugin layer to patch and nothing to conflict on update. The trade is that you get what the platform ships rather than what an ecosystem of 50,000 plugins can do. Before moving, check the one or two niche capabilities your current site depends on — that is where the gap shows, not in the everyday features. Blink for a business blog that has to rank and load fast without you maintaining anything: sitemap, robots.txt, JSON-LD structured data and Open Graph are in-product, plus an SEO panel that scores and fixes the live site. Squarespace is a reasonable choice for a personal blog where design matters more than control, but you cannot edit robots.txt or the sitemap, and Tooltester measured its mobile page-speed score at 28.94 — last of the twelve builders they tested. Webflow suits a publication with a designer on staff. Not without a rebuild of the storefront, but the data moves cleanly. Products, customers and orders export as CSV from WooCommerce and import into Shopify or another platform; the theme, checkout and any cart plugins do not come with them. Shopify is the right destination if the catalogue is the business — purpose-built checkout, POS, inventory and fulfilment, with card rates stepping down from 2.9% + 30¢ on Basic to 2.25% on Plus. If commerce is one section of a broader site, moving the whole site and running a simpler checkout is usually the cheaper path.

title: More Americans Have Access to Credit While Debt Growth Has Moderated
summary: New TransUnion (NYSE: TRU) research finds that consumer credit remains widely available despite economic uncertainty, while credit usage continues to grow at a pace largely consistent with inflation. TransUnion released the findings in conjunction with its Q2 2026 Credit Industry Insights Report (CIIR).Consumer access to credit continued to expa...
body_text: Chicago, 06 August 2026 | 05:50 AM America/Chicago More Americans Have Access to Credit While Debt Growth Has Moderated Q2 2026 TransUnion Credit Industry Insights Report shows balance growth, broader access and measured monthly payment pressure New TransUnion (NYSE: TRU) research finds that consumer credit remains widely available despite economic uncertainty, while credit usage continues to grow at a pace largely consistent with inflation. TransUnion released the findings in conjunction with its Q2 2026 Credit Industry Insights Report (CIIR). Consumer access to credit continued to expand in Q2 2026, with just under 262 million consumers carrying a credit balance. Total outstanding balances also grew steadily, reflecting broader credit participation and borrowing patterns consistent with recent years. “ This continued expansion in credit access shows that lenders are still extending credit broadly across the market. Lenders are managing risk through the use of strategies such as smaller credit lines, which allows them to continue expanding access to credit while navigating a complex economic environment. Jason Laky, executive vice president and head of financial services for TransUnion „ Growth in Total Balances and Credit Access Has Remained Steady Q2 2026 YoY 2025-2026 3-year CAGR* 2023-2026 Total Outstanding Balances $18.6 Trillion +2.8% +3.0% Number of Consumers With a Balance 261.7 million +2.4% +1.9% *Compound annual growth rate Source: TransUnion US consumer credit database Nevertheless, the expansion of credit access does not appear to have resulted in materially greater portfolio risk to lenders, even amid ongoing affordability pressures. While borrower-level credit card delinquency rates increased year over year (YoY), balance-level delinquency rates (1.98% in Q2 2026) are relatively flat, dropping by 2 basis points for the period. Average non-mortgage minimum payments – the average total amount due per month for all credit accounts in wallet except mortgage – have been modest across all credit risk tiers, up between 1 and 3 percent YoY for all except the prime tier (+3.5%). This indicates that debt obligations have increased at a manageable pace for most borrowers, and generally below the recent rate of inflation. Together, these trends indicate that broader credit availability has not led to excessive consumer debt burdens. Non-mortgage Minimum Payments Have Grown Slowly YoY Across All Risk Tiers YoY 2025-2026 4-year CAGR* 2022-2026 Subprime 1.3% 5.5% Near Prime 2.2% 6.1% Prime 3.5% 6.7% Prime Plus 1.8% 5.7% Super Prime 2.3% 6.8% *Compound annual growth rate Source: TransUnion US consumer credit database “While affordability pressures continue to weigh on many households, consumers appear to be managing credit obligations with relative discipline, as evidenced by modest growth in non-mortgage minimum payments and generally stable balance-level delinquency rates,” said Michele Raneri, vice president and head of U.S. research and consulting at TransUnion. “Although some consumers may be experiencing financial challenges, the broader credit picture suggests that balance growth has generally remained aligned with consumers’ ability to service their debt.” To learn more about the latest consumer credit trends, register for the Q2 2026 Quarterly Credit Industry Insights Report webinar . Read on for more specific insights about credit cards, personal loans, auto loans and mortgages. New bankcard credit lines grow as lenders implement strategic growth Q2 2026 CIIR Credit Card Summary · Bankcard originations rose 11.8% YoY to 20.6 million, marking a sixth consecutive quarter of growth and a Q1 record. Growth continued to be led by subprime and super prime borrowers, though the pace moderated from recent highs. · Total bankcard balances increased 4.4% YoY to $1.14 trillion, while lenders returned to a more growth-oriented strategy. title: The Missing Piece in a Strong Cybersecurity Strategy
summary: Read the latest AI news and insights on OpenTools.
body_text: Strong cybersecurity planning usually includes scanners, policies, response playbooks, training, and layered controls. Even then, breaches often begin with known weaknesses that linger after detection. The missing piece is verified closure. Understanding why that gap persists helps teams build a stronger defense. The difference often comes down to how discovery, action, and proof connect in daily operations. Platforms like Nagomi Security help close that gap by connecting exposure data, asset importance, control behavior, and completed fixes. Without that loop, busy teams can reduce ticket counts while reachable attack paths remain open. The areas below outline where that breakdown happens and how to address it. Each section focuses on a specific point where strategy and execution tend to separate. Why Coverage Breaks Most organizations already collect more exposure signals than staff can review. Each tool describes assets, permissions, vulnerabilities, and failed controls in its own language. A platform such as Nagomi Security belongs in this discussion because modern defense depends on correlating those signals, testing protection, and proving closure across existing systems. The hard part is deciding which open path creates real business danger today. More Data Is Not Enough More findings do not automatically improve judgment. Extra dashboards can bury urgent exposure under noise, especially when asset value and control status are unclear. Security staff need sharper answers, not larger queues. Useful reporting should show what changed, why exposure increased, which defense failed, and what fix would remove the most risk. Exposure Paths Matter Attackers usually combine small openings. Weak identity settings, exposed services, missing patches, and permissive access can form one usable route. A minor issue may become serious when it supports lateral movement. Strategy should review connected paths rather than isolated findings. That view helps teams recognize which combinations allow intrusion, privilege gain, or data access. Prioritization Needs Proof Risk scoring helps, but a number cannot replace evidence. Teams need to know whether a weakness is reachable, exploitable, or blocked by a working control. Otherwise, work may follow loud alerts instead of actual danger. Better prioritization weighs asset sensitivity, exposure depth, defensive coverage, and likely attacker behavior, following sound risk management principles before assigning urgency. Existing Controls Need Testing Deployed controls can fail quietly. Firewall rules drift, endpoint agents miss devices, identity policies lose scope, and scanner coverage ages. A mature strategy tests whether protection still works against current exposure. Verified performance gives leaders stronger risk signals and prevents false confidence based on installation alone. Closure Beats Ticket Counts A closed ticket is administrative evidence, not technical proof. A patch may install while a dangerous route remains available. A configuration change may pass review but fail under real conditions. Strong teams confirm closure from live systems. Verified remediation carries more weight than workflow status because it shows risk was actually reduced. Automation Needs Guardrails Automation can shorten investigation and remove repetitive triage. Human authority still matters where changes affect users, production systems, or regulated data. A sound model lets automation gather evidence, recommend actions, and confirm results. People should approve sensitive fixes, weigh tradeoffs, and intervene when business context changes the answer. Business Context Changes Priority Every exposed asset does not carry equal consequence. A lab server differs from an identity provider, payment service, or patient record system. Business context translates technical exposure into operational risk. Customer impact, revenue dependency, legal duty, and service criticality should shape remediation order. This connection helps leaders fund work that protects what matters most. Speed Requires Fewer Handoffs Exposure work often slows when every step crosses another team. Security identifies the issue, infrastructure reviews ownership, application staff judge impact, and operations schedule change. Delay grows with each handoff. Shared evidence reduces friction. Clear ownership, approved fix options, and verified outcomes help teams move from discovery to closure with less waiting. Metrics Should Show Risk Reduction Traditional metrics count open findings, overdue patches, and alert volume. Those numbers help manage workload, but they may miss real exposure. Stronger reporting tracks verified closures, removed attack paths, repaired control gaps, and time from discovery to validation. Leaders need measures that show whether practical risk is shrinking. The Human Factor People remain central to sound security decisions. Analysts recognize odd patterns, business constraints, and operational risk that tools may miss. Still, expert time should not be spent sorting duplicate alerts. Teams gain more value when staff review well‑evidenced cases, approve meaningful changes, and investigate signals that require judgment. Building the Missing Link The missing piece is a disciplined operating loop. Discovery finds exposure. Investigation explains business risk. Action removes the path. Validation proves the fix held. Each stage should carry context into the next. When that loop works, separate controls become a coordinated defense program rather than a collection of disconnected tools. Conclusion Cybersecurity becomes stronger when it moves from visibility to verified closure. Tools, controls, and skilled teams all matter, but their value depends on coordinated action. Leaders should ask whether exposures are discovered, explained, fixed, and validated before attackers can use them. The missing piece is not another list of findings. It is a repeatable operating loop that turns risk knowledge into confirmed reduction.

title: Additive Manufacturing in the Automotive Industry
summary: Learn how additive manufacturing transforms automotive production, from rapid prototyping to end use parts, tooling, and on demand customization.
body_text: Challenges to Mass Adoption The savings can be substantial. For example: Karsan reduced production costs by up to 80% by bringing AM component production in-house Roush saved 35% compared to injection molding on a low-volume part W. Speaker cut fixture production time by 89%, lowering both tooling costs and turnaround Challenges to Mass Adoption Additive manufacturing has earned a real place in automotive manufacturing, but it isn't a universal replacement for traditional methods. Like any process, it has a sweet spot, and knowing where that is matters as much as knowing what it can do. Per Part Cost at High Volumes At high volumes, injection molding and stamping are still hard to beat on cost. Once the tooling is made, the per-part cost drops low and stays there. AM makes more sense on the other end of the spectrum, prototypes, tooling, replacement parts, and low-volume runs where that upfront tooling investment is hard to justify in the first place. [H3] Print Speed and Throughput Although additive manufacturing technologies continue to improve, producing thousands or millions of identical parts is still faster with many conventional manufacturing processes. AM is often used where flexibility, speed to market, or design freedom are more important than maximum production volume. Certification and Quality Assurance Every part in a vehicle has to clear strict quality and performance bars, and additive parts are no exception. As AM works its way into production, processes like Production Part Approval Process (PPAP) exist to confirm a printed part actually meets the engineering standard it's supposed to. PPAP validates that a manufacturing process can consistently produce parts to engineering specifications. For additively manufactured components, that means documenting material properties, dimensional accuracy, and process repeatability across production runs. Stratasys Direct supports full PPAP workflows for production-grade 3D-printed parts. Material Property Limitations Materials keep improving, but there's still no single AM material that works for everything. Strength, heat resistance, durability, chemical resistance, surface finish, engineers have to weigh all of it before picking one. Choosing the right material ends up mattering just as much as choosing the right process.

title: AI Data Warehouses for Insurance, Manufacturing, and Operations
summary: How insurance, manufacturing, and operations teams can connect records, documents, and workflows into a governed AI data foundation across complex enterprises.
body_text: Insurance, manufacturing, and operations teams all work across structured systems and messy operational context. Claims and policies sit beside adjuster notes and correspondence. Production metrics sit beside maintenance logs and supplier emails. An operating review combines ERP data, tickets, documents, and decisions. An AI data warehouse can connect those sources into a governed context layer. The goal is not to replace a policy system, ERP, MES, or ticketing platform. It is to make authorized information easier to find, relate, explain, and use in a supervised workflow while preserving source permissions and evidence. o11’s Memory product page describes continuously indexing approved files, email, calendars, CRM, ERP, notes, templates, market data, and systems of record into permission-aware context. That architecture can apply beyond financial services, provided each industry defines its own entities, source authorities, retention, and approval controls. The shared pattern across three industries Pattern Insurance Manufacturing Operations Structured source Policy, claim, premium, reserve ERP, MES, inventory, quality Tickets, orders, workforce, finance Unstructured source Adjuster notes, reports, correspondence Maintenance logs, supplier emails, work instructions Meeting notes, SOPs, incident reports Core entity Policy, claim, customer, asset Plant, line, SKU, supplier Process, site, vendor, workstream Recurring output Claim review, underwriting brief Plant review, quality packet Operating review, risk update Main control Privacy, coverage, claims authority Safety, quality, traceability Role, site, process, escalation The nouns differ, but the architecture is similar: connect sources, resolve entities, preserve access, track freshness, show evidence, and route decisions to owners. Insurance use cases Claims context A claim may involve the policy, endorsements, loss notice, adjuster notes, photos, invoices, correspondence, and prior claims. A connected workflow can help an authorized adjuster locate the relevant record family and prepare a review packet. The system should distinguish extracted facts from coverage interpretation. A policy clause may be clear while the applicability to a particular loss requires professional review. Sources should include policy version and effective date. Underwriting and renewal Underwriters may combine applications, loss runs, inspections, financials, broker correspondence, and internal appetite rules. An AI workflow can surface missing materials and summarize changes since the prior renewal, but an underwriter owns the risk assessment and final decision. Regulatory and audit support Teams may need to retrieve evidence for a file review or control test. Source, version, access, and reviewer status matter as much as the summary. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework provides a public risk-management reference; it is not a substitute for insurance-specific obligations. Manufacturing use cases Production variance analysis An ERP or MES can show output, scrap, downtime, and margin. Maintenance logs, quality records, supplier notices, and shift notes may explain why the trend changed. A connected workflow can bring the numbers and the explanation together. Supplier and quality review Link purchase orders, supplier performance, inspection results, corrective-action plans, and correspondence. Preserve product, lot, plant, and date identifiers. A similar supplier name should not create a false relationship between facilities. Work-instruction retrieval Operators and engineers may need the current approved procedure, not an old PDF in a shared folder. Version and effective-date rules are essential. The system can help find the procedure, but the plant owner controls which instruction is active. Operations use cases Operating reviews An operating review often combines KPIs, tickets, project plans, incident reports, meeting notes, and commitments. A context layer can help prepare a draft with source-backed explanations and unresolved issues. Incident and root-cause support Connect alerts, tickets, runbooks, changes, communications, and post-incident reviews. The system can organize evidence and similar incidents, but the incident commander or process owner must validate the timeline and action plan. Vendor and process management Combine contracts, performance data, invoices, tickets, and email. This helps teams see the full relationship while preserving the distinction between an approved contract term and an informal request. A reusable architecture Layer Design choice Control Source registry Policy system, ERP/MES, ticketing, CRM, files, mail Owner and approved scope Entity model Policy/claim, plant/SKU, vendor/site, process/workstream Stable IDs and aliases Context index Records, documents, notes, tables, versions Freshness and status Evidence layer Page, record, table, cell, event, or ticket Source-backed claims Permission layer Team, site, matter, customer, role, or process Negative access tests Application layer Review, alert, brief, action, or system update Human owner and approval This is a foundation pattern, not a requirement to replace existing systems. In many deployments, the operational system remains the authority and the AI data warehouse supplies cross-system context. How to handle safety and sensitive data The risks differ by industry, but the controls are familiar: define what data is approved for indexing; separate personal, confidential, and operational sources; carry permissions into retrieval and output; label current and historical versions; show evidence behind material claims; log review and action state; and retain only what policy permits. For insurance, test personally identifiable and claim-sensitive data. For manufacturing, test plant and supplier boundaries. For operations, test site, customer, incident, and personnel restrictions. How o11 fits the broader model o11’s positioning is broader than a single industry. The product is intended to connect approved enterprise sources and apply context to research, decisions, drafting, analysis, and supervised action. The same product layer can support financial-services workflows and complex operational work, but the deployment must be grounded in domain-specific source definitions. The important promise is not that an AI system understands every industry automatically. It is that an organization can bring the context already present in its systems into a governed workflow without rebuilding the same connection for each question. Common failure modes Treating the operational system as complete context An ERP or policy record may be authoritative for a field but not explain the decision or exception. Connect narrative evidence without overriding the source of record. Ignoring version and effective dates The latest uploaded procedure or endorsement may not be the active one. Track status and effective period. Hiding uncertainty If the system has not indexed a shift note or cannot resolve a supplier identity, say so. Do not infer that missing evidence means no issue exists. Making actions autonomous too early Start with review packets, recommendations, and draft actions. Require approval before changing a system of record, notifying a customer, or making a safety-sensitive decision. Limitations and tradeoffs Industry data is often incomplete and locally defined. A policy term can depend on jurisdiction. A maintenance note can be informal. A production metric can change after a late adjustment. AI can organize the evidence but cannot remove those domain uncertainties. o11 can provide connected, permission-aware context, but it does not replace insurance authority, plant safety controls, quality management, operations ownership, or regulatory programs. Validate sources, retention, security, and approvals with domain experts. A pilot framework Choose one repeatable workflow in one business unit: define the question and output; list approved structured and unstructured sources; define entities, period, and authority; test authorized and unauthorized users; require evidence and human approval; and measure review time, exceptions, freshness, and corrections. Examples include a claim review, plant variance update, supplier-risk packet, or incident retrospective. Expand only after the first workflow demonstrates reliable source and permission behavior. Keep domain authority explicit Cross-industry platforms work best when the shared architecture is paired with local authority rules. In insurance, identify which policy version controls coverage and which source controls claim status. In manufacturing, identify whether ERP, MES, or a quality system controls a measure and how late adjustments are represented. In operations, identify which ticket, incident, or process owner can close an issue. Write these rules next to the workflow rather than burying them in a generic data dictionary. A user asking “what is current?” needs the domain’s current rule. The system should also expose when no source satisfies that rule, so missing authority becomes an escalation instead of a plausible answer. Measure the pilot by domain-relevant outcomes: claim-file review time and missing evidence for insurance; downtime explanation and corrective-action closure for manufacturing; incident-review time and overdue commitments for operations. Pair each metric with a quality check, such as version correctness, source citation, or owner approval, so speed does not reward unsafe shortcuts. Keep the initial deployment narrow enough to observe. One claims team, one plant, or one operations process produces better feedback than a company-wide index launched without local owners. Capture the source manifest, users, freshness expectation, and escalation path. When a result is wrong, classify the failure—missing source, stale record, entity mismatch, permission error, or interpretation—before changing the prompt or adding more data. Define the handoff to the system of record. A review packet may be generated in the context layer, but the approved claim status, maintenance action, or incident closure should be written only through the organization’s normal control. Record who accepted the recommendation, what evidence they saw, and whether the source system changed. This keeps AI assistance additive and makes it possible to reconcile the workflow with the operational record later. Also define the failure path. If a policy document is unavailable, a machine event is delayed, or a ticket lacks an owner, the workflow should stop or label the gap. Escalation is part of the design; it is not evidence that the system failed. The same rule applies to confidence. A claim summary with complete policy evidence can move to normal review, while a production explanation based on one unconfirmed shift note should remain provisional. Make confidence and missing evidence visible so the accountable operator can choose the next safe action. That distinction is especially important when an output could trigger a customer notice, safety response, reserve change, or corrective-action deadline. Frequently asked questions Is this the same as a BI platform? No. BI platforms are strong at modeled metrics and dashboards. An AI data warehouse can connect those metrics with documents, messages, records, relationships, and workflow context. Can o11 replace an ERP, MES, or policy system? No. Those systems remain systems of record. o11 is positioned as a connected context and workflow layer around approved sources. How should sensitive data be handled? Define approved sources, access groups, retention, citation visibility, and output sharing before indexing. Test negative access cases. What should insurance teams review first? Start with claims or renewal context where a clear adjuster or underwriter owns the review. Separate extracted policy facts from coverage interpretation. What should manufacturers review first? Production variance, supplier quality, or current work-instruction retrieval are useful pilots with measurable outputs and clear owners. What should operations teams review first? Choose an operating review, incident retrospective, or vendor-risk packet that combines metrics with narrative evidence. Sources and further reading o11 Memory: connected enterprise context o11 Enterprise NIST AI Risk Management Framework NIST Privacy Framework NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 W3C PROV-O provenance ontology The product description and claims in this article were reviewed against o11’s public product pages on 2026-08-14.

title: How the Envelope System Stops Overspending Before It Starts
summary: Learn how the envelope system prevents overspending by assigning money before you spend it. A proven budget method to control your finances.
body_text: A growing number of Americans are struggling to stay financially afloat, with 69% reporting living paycheck to paycheck, a four-year high and a sharp jump from 60% just one year prior, according to Debt.com's annual budgeting survey. That statistic demands a response. Therefore, if you have ever reached the end of the month and wondered where your money went, the envelope system may be the most practical tool available to fix that problem, starting with your very next paycheck. The envelope system is a proactive financial strategy: traditional budgeting tracks spending after it happens, while envelope budgeting assigns money before you spend it, and that shift alone changes financial behavior. This guide explains exactly what the envelope system is, how to set it up in physical or digital form, why the psychology behind it works, and which common mistakes to avoid. Key Takeaways Overspending is a structural problem, not a willpower problem: Nearly 2 in 5 Americans (39%) exceed their budget every month, while around 1 in 6 (15%) do it on a weekly basis. The envelope system creates a hard stop that prevents this by design, if you routinely run short before month-end, this method addresses the root cause structurally. Pre-allocation is the core mechanism: Envelope budgeting is a method where you divide your income into categories and allocate a fixed amount to each "envelope." Once the money inside runs out, spending in that category stops until the next budgeting cycle. Therefore, assign every dollar a category before you spend a single one. The psychology of cash is real: Research shows people spend 12-18% less when using cash versus cards, meaning switching just your highest-spending category to cash can produce measurable savings in month one. Digital formats work too: The envelope system can be implemented using physical cash envelopes or with modern digital apps for convenience, so a cashless lifestyle is not a barrier to entry. Debt stress is widespread: A combined 82% of Americans say they find the idea of being in debt stressful, according to YouGov's 2025 American financial attitudes survey. The envelope system attacks that stress at its source, because pre-allocated categories prevent new debt from forming in the first place. Quick-Start Prioritization Framework Not every reader starts from the same place. Use this table to find your best entry point before reading further. Your Situation Best Starting Format Effort Level Time to See Results Overspender in one or two categories Cash envelopes for those categories only Low 2-4 weeks Complete beginner to budgeting 5 physical envelopes for variable spending Low 1-2 months Mostly cashless lifestyle Digital envelope app Low-Medium 2-4 weeks Budget tracker who still overspends Hybrid: cash for problem categories, digital for the rest Medium 1 month Budgeting with a partner Shared digital envelope account Medium 1-2 months Start here if you are: A first-time budgeter: Begin with five physical cash envelopes covering groceries, gas, dining out, entertainment, and personal spending. Keep it simple so the habit forms before the categories multiply. Already using a budgeting app but still overspending: Add cash envelopes for your two biggest problem categories. The physical friction will produce a behavioral change that a screen notification cannot replicate. Living fully digitally: A dedicated digital envelope tool like Envelope by envelopebudgeting.com builds categorical budget limits directly into a checking account and debit card, making the system compatible with a fully cashless lifestyle. What the Envelope System Actually Is The Core Concept Cash stuffing, also called the envelope system, is a budgeting method where you put physical cash into envelopes, each labeled for a specific expense, to portion out your monthly income. The rule is simple: once the money in an envelope is gone, you stop spending in that category. There is no credit line to tap, no overdraft to fall back on. The limit is physical and immediate. The system works because it converts abstract numbers into visible, tangible limits. Knowing you have "budgeted $400 for groceries" is different from seeing four $100 bills in an envelope and watching them disappear. That visibility is what separates the envelope method from spreadsheets and apps that simply log what you have already spent. A Brief History The envelope system, also known as the envelope budgeting method or cash stuffing, is a popular personal budgeting method for visualizing and maintaining a flexible budget. The key idea is to prioritize cash income to meet separate categories of household expenses in physically separate envelopes. The method was made widely popular by finance personality and radio host Dave Ramsey, though its roots stretch back well before his public advocacy of the approach. The underlying principle has outlasted every financial trend of the past half-century because it targets a permanent feature of human behavior: people spend more when limits are invisible. Physical vs. Digital: What Has Changed In 2025, digital envelope budgeting evolves into a powerful money management framework that blends the discipline of old-school cash envelopes with the intelligence of modern financial apps. It connects to bank accounts digital wallets, and credit cards for real-time money management. The core principle is identical regardless of format. If you want to run the system entirely digitally, Envelope by envelopebudgeting.com builds the categorical envelope structure directly into a checking account. The Psychology Behind Why It Works The Pain of Paying The reason the envelope system outperforms a simple written budget comes down to neuroscience. As Carnegie Mellon professor George Loewenstein put it, "Credit cards effectively anesthetize the pain of paying. You swipe the card and it doesn't feel like you're giving anything up to make the purchase, unlike paying cash where you have to hand over bills." In a 2008 paper in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, researchers Priya Raghubir and Joydeep Srivastava found significant differences in spending based on how shoppers pay for things. In one study, participants were willing to spend $175 to throw a Thanksgiving party when using a credit card, but only $145 when using cash. That is a 21% difference from the payment method alone, before any budgeting discipline enters the picture. Therefore, if you have a category where you chronically overspend, switching it to cash envelopes is the highest-leverage change you can make. Why Visible Limits Change Behavior Cash payments have high psychological salience because they involve handing over physical money, making people realize what they have to pay. Precisely because of the pain of paying, consumers who use cash are more inclined to consider costs and less likely to focus purely on benefits than those who pay using a credit card. Pro Tip: If going fully cash-based feels unrealistic, use the hybrid approach. Run cash envelopes only for the one or two categories where you overspend most, groceries, dining out, or personal shopping are common culprits. The behavioral shift in those categories alone is often enough to correct the monthly shortfall. How to Set Up the Envelope System in Five Steps Step 1, Calculate Your Net Income Everything flows from your net (not gross) earnings, the money you have left after taxes and withholdings. Budgeting from your gross income is one of the most common beginner mistakes, because it sets limits you cannot actually meet. Add up all monthly income sources after tax. That total is your ceiling for the month, and not a dollar more. Step 2, List Your Spending Categories List your monthly expenses including fixed expenses like rent, auto payment, and utilities, as well as variable expenses such as groceries and entertainment. Next to each expense, jot down which category it belongs in and how much you are budgeting. The system is built around variable expenses, the categories where spending fluctuates and willpower fails. Fixed bills like rent, insurance, and loan payments stay in your checking account on autopay. Step 3, Set Realistic Limits If you averaged $500 per month on groceries, do not set your envelope to $300. Try $450 first. Small, sustainable cuts beat dramatic ones that you cannot maintain. Base your initial limits on three months of actual spending data, then reduce gradually. The goal in the first month is to learn your real spending patterns, not to perform an ideal budget. Step 4, Fund and Label Your Envelopes For physical envelopes: withdraw the total cash needed for variable categories on payday, then divide it into each labeled envelope. Typically, write the name and average monthly cost of each category on the front of an envelope. Then, either once a month or when you get paid, put the allocated amount in cash into the envelope. For digital envelopes: log into your app or digital account, create each spending category, and assign the budgeted amount. Step 5, Track and Adjust Monthly Review your budget regularly and make adjustments as needed. What worked last month might not work for the next month, and that is acceptable. A successful budget is one that evolves with you. If a category is consistently empty by week three, that is data, either your limit is too low or your habits need attention. Either way, you now know. Pro Tip: The most common setup mistake is starting with too many envelopes. Five to seven categories is plenty for month one. Add more once the habit is established. Complexity kills consistency in the early weeks. Common Envelope System Mistakes and How to Fix Them Mixing Fixed and Variable Expenses Sometimes people mix up fixed and variable expense types by accident. If you put too much cash into a flexible category, you might later find you do not have enough for important bills. A common mistake is mixing a regular car payment with an occasional repair, which throws the whole budgeting system off balance. The fix: keep fixed bills on autopay from your main checking account and only fund variable categories with envelopes. Forgetting Annual Expenses Many people only focus on monthly expenses, overlooking annual ones like car registration. To ensure you have money available when it is due, create an envelope for these annual expenses as well. It is far easier to add $10 or $20 to that envelope each month than to find the full $120 or $240 immediately. Think of it like prepaying your own irregular bills in small monthly installments. Setting Unrealistic Limits and Giving Up When starting the envelope method it is easy to make a few common mistakes. One is setting unrealistic spending limits that are too hard to follow. Another is not being flexible when unexpected expenses pop up. Giving up after one bad month is also a frequent pitfall. The system requires a few months of iteration before the category amounts feel natural. Treat month one as a rough draft, not a final answer. Pro Tip: If you are unsure which format suits you, run a hybrid for the first month. Use physical cash for the one or two categories where you overspend most and manage the rest digitally. The cash friction in your problem categories will produce the biggest behavioral change with the least disruption to how you currently live. The Envelope System in a Digital World The most common objection to the envelope system in 2026 is that most transactions happen on cards or online. While traditional envelope budgeting relies on cash envelopes, modern technology offers a digital alternative. You do not have to carry wads of cash to use this budgeting system. The traditional envelope method - dividing your paycheck into labeled cash envelopes such as rent, groceries, and entertainment, has helped millions stay disciplined for decades. The modern evolution replaces paper cash envelopes with virtual budgeting categories inside apps, connecting to bank accounts, digital wallets, and credit cards for real-time money management. A strong option for those who want a fully integrated digital experience is Envelope by envelopebudgeting.com, which is designed for those who want their budget connected to their checking account and debit card, combining budgeting with banking so you can organize your money into digital envelopes and use envelope budgeting without carrying cash. The behavioral advantage of cash, the "pain of paying", can be partially replicated digitally when a spending limit produces a hard stop at the point of purchase rather than a retroactive notification. The key is that the limit must feel real before the transaction, not after it. Frequently Asked Questions What is the envelope system in simple terms? Envelope budgeting is a budgeting method where you divide your income into categories and allocate a fixed amount of money to each category using separate "envelopes." Once the money inside an envelope runs out, spending in that category stops. The method works with physical cash or a digital app, and the core rule is identical in both formats. Does the envelope system still work if I rarely use cash? Yes. Envelope budgeting is a simple strategy that may help you control your spending by giving a job to every dollar you earn, and you can use this budgeting system with physical envelopes or more modern digital budgeting apps. Tools like Envelope apply categorical limits directly to debit card spending, making the method compatible with a fully cashless lifestyle. How many envelopes should I start with? Divide your after-bills spending money into five to ten envelopes, physical or digital, for categories like groceries, dining out, gas, and entertainment. Stay within each envelope's limit. When it is empty, you are done until next month. Starting with five to seven is the recommendation for month one, with more added as the habit becomes automatic. What should I do if an envelope runs out before month-end? One of the main advantages of envelope budgeting is making sure each envelope has the right amount for its category. While you can move money between envelopes, this is a flexible system; you cannot keep borrowing from other envelopes. If you notice you are doing it to compensate for the same envelope month after month, it pays to look at the root of the problem and fix it. That recurring shortfall is a signal to either raise the category limit or address the spending pattern directly. How is envelope budgeting different from just tracking expenses? The envelope system has outlasted decades of personal finance trends because it solves the real problem: most people do not overspend because they lack financial knowledge; they overspend because nothing stops them in the moment. The envelope system creates that stop. Expense tracking tells you what happened. The envelope system prevents the problem before it occurs. Start With One Envelope The envelope system is one of the few personal finance methods that works precisely because it is simple. You do not need software, a financial advisor, or a high income. You need a clear picture of your take-home pay, a handful of spending categories, and the willingness to stop spending when a category empties. Following a 12-year period of sustained improvements in financial capability, the FINRA Foundation's 2025 National Financial Capability Study reveals an overall pattern of decline in U.S. adults' ability to make ends meet and save for emergencies. The external pressures are real, but a system that assigns every dollar before it is spent is one of the most direct responses available. Start with one envelope this pay period. title: Climb Signs Distribution Agreement with Harmonic Security to Help Secure Mid-Market & Enterprise AI Adoption
summary: Eatontown, NJ (August 5, 2026) – Climb, an international specialty technology distributor and wholly owned subsidiary of Climb Global Solutions,...
body_text: Eatontown, NJ (August 5, 2026) – Climb, an international specialty technology distributor and wholly owned subsidiary of Climb Global Solutions, Inc. (NASDAQ: CLMB), today announced a distribution agreement with Harmonic Security, the AI governance and control platform for the AI-first workforce. Under the agreement, Climb will offer the Harmonic AI security platform to its network of value-added resellers (VARs) and managed service providers (MSPs) across the United States. Employees have moved past chatting with AI. They are handling work to it, kicking off agentic workflows in tools like Claude Cowork, Claude Code, and OpenAI’s agents that read files, run code, and act across enterprise systems on their behalf. That opens two gaps most security teams cannot see: agents taking actions no one reviewed, and intellectual property flowing out to AI providers with every prompt, file, and repository they touch. Harmonic Security governs this new layer of work across browsers, desktops, and the agentic AI layer, giving teams visibility into what employees and their agents are doing and stopping risky actions and IP leakage at the moment they happen. The agreement with Climb gives resellers and MSPs a direct route to a platform built for how AI is actually used, not legacy tooling retrofitted for it. For channel partners, it opens a fast-growing category their customers are already asking about. “Employees have moved past chatting with AI. They are running agents in tools like Claude Code and Cowork that take real actions and pull in real intellectual property, and most security teams have no view of it,” said Alastair Paterson, CEO and co-founder of Harmonic Security. “Climb gives us reach into the resellers and MSPs serving exactly these organizations. Together we can help teams govern workforce use of AI, from the actions their agents take to the IP that leaves the building, without slowing the work down.” “Our partners are fielding urgent questions about AI agents acting inside customer environments and pulling company IP into AI providers, and until now they have not had a purpose-built answer,” said Charles Bass, Chief Alliance Officer at Climb. “Adding Harmonic Security to our line card gives VARs and MSPs a way to meet that demand with a platform designed for the problem, backed by Climb’s financing, quoting, and relationship-led channel support.” Those interested in distribution services and solutions should contact Climb by phone at +1.800.847.7078 +1.888.523.7777 (Canada), or by email at Sales@ClimbCS.com About Climb Climb is a global specialty technology distributor focusing on Security, Data Management, Connectivity, Storage & HCI, Virtualization & Cloud, and Software & Application Lifecycle. Climb is committed to transforming distribution by providing emerging and established IT technologies, flexible financing, real-time quoting, best of breed channel operations, speed to market, and exceptional service to our partners worldwide. Climb is a wholly owned subsidiary of Climb Global Solutions (NASDAQ: CLMB). Experience the Climb difference and learn how our people first approach empowers VARs and MSPs to grow, scale, and accelerate their business. Visit www.ClimbCS.com , call 1-800-847-7078, and connect with us on LinkedIn ! For Media & PR inquiries contact: Climb Media Relations media@ClimbCS.com Investor Relations Contact: Elevate IR Sean Mansouri, CFA T: 720-330-2829 CLMB@elevate-ir.com About Harmonic Security Harmonic Security is the AI governance and control platform for the AI-first workforce. As employees adopt AI tools and hand work to autonomous agents in products like Claude Cowork, Claude Code, and OpenAI’s agents, Harmonic gives security teams visibility and control across browsers, desktops, and the agentic AI layer, including MCP clients and servers. Harmonic stops risky agent actions and prevents intellectual property from leaking to AI providers, without blocking the tools and workflows employees rely on to do their jobs. Learn more at http://www.harmonic.security/ For Media & PR inquiries contact: Press contact david@harmonic.security Download the Press Release
